---
title: "Architecture Test — WebGeoDS Stack"
subtitle: "Manual verification of runtime, R/Python editor, map, and OJS reactivity"
---

This page is not an automated test: the entire stack (WebR, Pyodide, MapLibre) runs entirely **in the browser** via WebAssembly, so it must be opened with `quarto preview` (or in the published HTML file) and verified by eye, clicking the "▶ Run" buttons and observing the output of each cell.

::: {.callout-note}
**Rewrite of August 26, 2026 — almost all cells now go through the Lua filter.** With support for `#| package: ...` added the same day (see `webgeods-cells.lua`), there is no longer any R/Python code cell that the filter can't generate — this page has therefore been rewritten to use `{.webgeods-python}`/`{.webgeods-r}` wherever possible, instead of the hand-written `<div>` + `<script>` boilerplate that populated it before. Only three things remain hand-written, for different structural reasons: **§1** (no code cell, just buttons and a status panel), **§9** (demonstrates the manual `CellOutput` methods — `waiting()`/`success()`/`append()` called directly in a custom `onRun` — something the filter can't generate, since it always produces the same fixed `onRun` "run the code, show the result") and **§10-§11** (the map: these aren't R/Python code cells, `WebGeoDS.Map` doesn't go through `WebGeoDS.CodeCell`). All the others — **§2-§8, §12-§14, §15, §16** — are generated by the `{.webgeods-python}`/`{.webgeods-r}` syntax (declared in `_quarto.yml`).

Two direct consequences of this change, worth keeping in mind while reading the sections below: (1) the waiting message shown during execution is now always the fixed one generated by the filter ("Running..."), no longer the descriptive messages previously hand-written cell by cell (e.g. "Loading webR + the sf package, up to a minute the first time...") — the equivalent information stays in the section text, above the cell, no longer in the widget itself; (2) where a package is needed (§3, §6), it is declared with a `#| package: ...` line at the top of the cell body instead of the `{ packages: [...] }` option passed by hand to `WebGeoDS.Python.run`/`WebGeoDS.R.run`.

**§15** also gathers the filter's complete history — the mandatory dotted syntax, the (abandoned) attempt to have the filter generate reactive OJS directly, and the long-standing `viewof`/`Generators.input` bug that led to `WebGeoDS.getCellValue()` — into a single section, replacing the two separate sections (§10 and §16) of this page's previous version.
:::

## 1. Runtime Manager — lifecycle and observable state

Verify: initial state `idle` for both engines, `loading → ready` transitions (or `error`), `statuschange` event received in real time, `terminate*()` bringing the state back to `idle`.

<div id="runtime-status" class="webgeods-output" style="margin-bottom: 12px;">
  <span class="webgeods-log-waiting"># Status not yet detected…</span>
</div>

<p>
  <button id="btn-load-python" class="webgeods-run-btn">▶ Load Python (Pyodide)</button>
  <button id="btn-load-r" class="webgeods-run-btn">▶ Load R (webR)</button>
  <button id="btn-term-python" class="webgeods-run-btn" style="background:#8b949e;">■ Terminate Python</button>
  <button id="btn-term-r" class="webgeods-run-btn" style="background:#8b949e;">■ Terminate R</button>
  <button id="btn-term-all" class="webgeods-run-btn" style="background:#f85149;">■ Terminate all</button>
</p>

<script>
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => {

  const statusEl = document.getElementById("runtime-status");

  const render = () => {
    const s = window.WebGeoDS.Runtime.status();
    statusEl.textContent = `python: ${s.python}    |    r: ${s.r}`;
  };

  render();

  window.WebGeoDS.Runtime.addEventListener("statuschange", render);

  document.getElementById("btn-load-python").onclick = () =>
    window.WebGeoDS.Runtime.python().catch(err => alert("Error loading Python: " + err.message));

  document.getElementById("btn-load-r").onclick = () =>
    window.WebGeoDS.Runtime.r().catch(err => alert("Error loading R: " + err.message));

  document.getElementById("btn-term-python").onclick = () =>
    window.WebGeoDS.Runtime.terminatePython();

  document.getElementById("btn-term-r").onclick = () =>
    window.WebGeoDS.Runtime.terminateR();

  document.getElementById("btn-term-all").onclick = () =>
    window.WebGeoDS.Runtime.terminateAll();

});
</script>

## 2. Python — basic execution

Verify: lazy loading of Pyodide on the first Run, `print()` captured in `stdout`, the value of the last expression shown as `Output: ...`. Cell generated by the Lua filter (`{.webgeods-python #cell-py-base}`).

```{.webgeods-python #cell-py-base}
import sys
print("Python", sys.version.split()[0])
21 * 2
```

## 3. Python — extra packages and a non-natively-serializable value

Verify: `#| package: numpy` at the top of the cell (the filter translates it into the already-existing `packages` option of `WebGeoDS.Python.run`), multiple `stdout` lines in order, and an edge case — the last expression is a NumPy `ndarray`, which Pyodide returns as a `PyProxy`. Worth observing how `formatValue()` (in `code-cell.js`) handles a value that isn't a native JS object.

```{.webgeods-python #cell-py-numpy}
#| package: numpy
import numpy as np
valori = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print("Mean:", np.mean(valori))
print("Standard deviation:", np.std(valori))
np.array(valori)
```

## 4. Python — error handling

Verify: an unhandled Python exception in `onRun` must be caught by `WebGeoDSCodeCell.run()`'s automatic fallback and shown with `output.error(...)`.

```{.webgeods-python #cell-py-error}
1 / 0
```

## 5. R — basic execution

Verify: lazy loading of webR, `cat()` captured in `stdout`, the last expression (`1:5`) auto-printed by R and therefore already visible via `stdout` — no duplicate `Output: ...` expected (see §7).

```{.webgeods-r #cell-r-base}
saluto <- "Hello from R!"
cat(saluto, "\n")
1:5
```

## 6. R — the `sf` package (regression check: duplicate format)

Regression check for the August 24, 2026 fix to `code-cell.js`: the `sf` object is auto-printed by R (it ends up in `stdout`), and previously it was *also* shown as a raw JSON dump of the coordinates in a separate `Output: ...` line. With the fix, since `stdout` isn't empty, that line must not appear: **only the `sf` table printed by R should be visible**, in a single format. `#| package: sf` here replaces the installation that used to be done by hand before the Run — the first execution of this cell may take up to a minute to download the package.

```{.webgeods-r #cell-r-sf}
#| package: sf
library(sf)
citta <- data.frame(
  name = c("Rome", "Milan", "Naples"),
  lon  = c(12.4964, 9.19, 14.2681),
  lat  = c(41.9028, 45.4642, 40.8518)
)
punti <- st_as_sf(citta, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
punti
```

## 7. R — final value not auto-printed (fallback `Output: ...`)

Verify the opposite branch of the §6 fix: when `stdout` is empty (here, `invisible()` suppresses the auto-print), the `Output: ...` line must still appear — otherwise the execution would show nothing.

```{.webgeods-r #cell-r-invisible}
x <- 10
y <- 32
invisible(x + y)
```

## 8. R — error handling

Verify: `stop()` in R must propagate as a JS exception and end up in `WebGeoDSCodeCell.run()`'s `output.error(...)` fallback.

```{.webgeods-r #cell-r-error}
stop("intentional test error")
```

## 9. `CellOutput` — manual logging methods (`waiting` / `success` / `append`)

Verify independent of the R/Python runtimes: `waiting()` and `success()` clear the previous content (`clear()` before each log), while `append()` appends an extra DOM node without clearing anything. This cell remains hand-written — the filter always generates the same fixed `onRun` ("run the code, show the result"), whereas here the `onRun` calls `CellOutput`'s methods directly and doesn't execute any R/Python code at all.

<div id="cell-output-methods"></div>

<script>
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => {
  new window.WebGeoDS.CodeCell("cell-output-methods", {
    language: "python",
    initialCode: `# this code is not executed: onRun deliberately ignores it`,
    onRun: async (code, output) => {

      output.waiting("Step 1/3 — waiting() test...");
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 500));

      output.waiting("Step 2/3 — new log, the previous one should disappear (clear())...");
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 500));

      output.success("Step 3/3 — success() with detail", "This line comes from the `detail` parameter.");

      const badge = document.createElement("div");
      badge.textContent = "✓ DOM node added via output.append(), without clear()";
      badge.style.marginTop = "8px";
      badge.style.color = "#7ee787";
      output.append(badge);

      return "ok";
    }
  });
});
</script>

## 10. Map — `WebGeoDS.Map` / MapLibre

Verify: lazy loading of MapLibre (only once, CSS included), automatic geometry-type detection (`Point → circle`, `LineString → line`, `Polygon → fill`), default paint vs. custom paint, `fitToData`, `setGeoJSON` (update-or-create), `removeGeoJSON`, `resize()`, and error handling for a duplicate source. This isn't an R/Python code cell: `WebGeoDS.Map` doesn't go through `WebGeoDS.CodeCell`, so the Lua filter doesn't apply here — it remains hand-written as before.

<div id="map-resize-wrapper" style="width: 100%; max-width: 900px;">
  <div id="map-test"></div>
</div>

<p>
  <button id="btn-map-update" class="webgeods-run-btn">▶ Add Turin (setGeoJSON)</button>
  <button id="btn-map-remove" class="webgeods-run-btn">▶ Remove link (removeGeoJSON)</button>
  <button id="btn-map-resize" class="webgeods-run-btn">▶ Narrow/widen container + resize()</button>
  <button id="btn-map-duplicate" class="webgeods-run-btn" style="background:#f85149;">▶ Test error: duplicate source</button>
</p>

<p id="map-resize-status" class="webgeods-output" style="margin-top: 8px;">
  <span class="webgeods-log-waiting"># resize() not yet tested</span>
</p>

<script>
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", async () => {

  const cittaGeoJSON = {
    type: "FeatureCollection",
    features: [
      { type: "Feature", properties: { name: "Rome" },   geometry: { type: "Point", coordinates: [12.4964, 41.9028] } },
      { type: "Feature", properties: { name: "Milan" }, geometry: { type: "Point", coordinates: [9.19, 45.4642] } },
      { type: "Feature", properties: { name: "Naples" }, geometry: { type: "Point", coordinates: [14.2681, 40.8518] } }
    ]
  };

  const collegamentoGeoJSON = {
    type: "Feature",
    properties: { name: "Rome–Milan–Naples" },
    geometry: {
      type: "LineString",
      coordinates: [[12.4964, 41.9028], [9.19, 45.4642], [14.2681, 40.8518]]
    }
  };

  const areaGeoJSON = {
    type: "Feature",
    properties: { name: "Test area" },
    geometry: {
      type: "Polygon",
      coordinates: [[[12.0, 41.0], [13.2, 41.0], [13.2, 42.3], [12.0, 42.3], [12.0, 41.0]]]
    }
  };

  const map = new window.WebGeoDS.Map("map-test", {
    center: [12.4964, 41.9028],
    zoom: 5
  });

  await map.ready();

  // Read-only hook for smoke-test.mjs: verifying "Turin appeared" by
  // reading canvas pixels isn't practical in an automated script,
  // while the source's GeoJSON is. Lives only in this test page, not
  // in the public library.
  window.__webgeodsTestMap = map;

  await map.addGeoJSON("citta", cittaGeoJSON);               // auto-detect -> circle
  await map.addGeoJSON("collegamento", collegamentoGeoJSON); // auto-detect -> line
  await map.addGeoJSON("area-test", areaGeoJSON, {            // custom paint
    paint: {
      "fill-color": "#58a6ff",
      "fill-opacity": 0.25,
      "fill-outline-color": "#58a6ff"
    }
  });

  await map.fitToData(cittaGeoJSON, { padding: 60 });

  document.getElementById("btn-map-update").onclick = async () => {
    const aggiornato = {
      ...cittaGeoJSON,
      features: [
        ...cittaGeoJSON.features,
        { type: "Feature", properties: { name: "Turin" }, geometry: { type: "Point", coordinates: [7.6869, 45.0703] } }
      ]
    };
    await map.setGeoJSON("citta", aggiornato);
    await map.fitToData(aggiornato, { padding: 60 });
  };

  document.getElementById("btn-map-remove").onclick = async () => {
    await map.removeGeoJSON("collegamento");
  };

  // The original test only called map.resize() without ever changing
  // the container's dimensions: no visible effect to observe, so it
  // was impossible to distinguish "works but there's nothing to see"
  // from "doesn't work". Here the button toggles the container's
  // width — something that should already trigger WebGeoDS.Map's
  // internal ResizeObserver on its own — and then calls resize()
  // explicitly, reporting on screen whether the call succeeded or
  // threw an error.
  const resizeStatus = document.getElementById("map-resize-status");
  const resizeWrapper = document.getElementById("map-resize-wrapper");
  let wrapperNarrow = false;

  const logResize = (text, className) => {
    resizeStatus.innerHTML = "";
    const span = document.createElement("span");
    span.className = className;
    span.textContent = text;
    resizeStatus.appendChild(span);
  };

  document.getElementById("btn-map-resize").onclick = async () => {
    try {
      wrapperNarrow = !wrapperNarrow;
      resizeWrapper.style.maxWidth = wrapperNarrow ? "450px" : "900px";
      await map.resize();
      logResize(
        `✓ resize() executed without errors — container width now: ${resizeWrapper.style.maxWidth}`,
        "webgeods-log-success"
      );
    } catch (err) {
      logResize(`✗ resize() threw an error: ${err.message}`, "webgeods-log-error");
    }
  };

  document.getElementById("btn-map-duplicate").onclick = async () => {
    try {
      await map.addGeoJSON("citta", cittaGeoJSON);
      alert("BUG: addGeoJSON did not throw an error for a duplicate source");
    } catch (err) {
      alert("OK, expected error: " + err.message);
    }
  };

});
</script>

## 11. Map — custom style (`alidade_smooth.json`)

Verify the `style` option of `WebGeoDS.Map` with a local style file instead of the remote default `dark-matter-gl-style`, and reuse of the same MapLibre instance already loaded by §10 (no double loading of the library). Like §10, this isn't an R/Python code cell: it remains hand-written.

::: {.callout-important}
`alidade_smooth.json` points to vector tiles on `tiles.stadiamaps.com`: if the tiles don't show up but the console shows no errors from `WebGeoDS.Map`, an authentication/domain requirement on the Stadia Maps side is likely, not a problem with the WebGeoDS stack. The file was added to `resources:` in `_quarto.yml` so it gets copied alongside the published HTML (necessary: with `embed-resources: true` scripts get inlined, but a runtime `fetch()` to this JSON is still a request to an external file).
:::

## 12. Python — Web Worker: the UI stays responsive

Verify the most important change of this session: Pyodide now runs inside a dedicated Web Worker (see `pythonWorkerEntry()` in `runtime.js`), no longer on the main thread. The counter below increments every 300ms via `setInterval` on the page — if it stays still while the Python cell below is computing, the execution is still blocking the UI (regression); if it keeps ticking, the worker is doing its job.

<p>
  Page heartbeat (must keep rising even while a cell is running):
  <strong id="heartbeat-counter">0</strong>
</p>

```{.webgeods-python #cell-py-heavy}
# Heavy loop, deliberately slow: if the number below finishes in a
# fraction of a second or takes minutes, adjust it to get a few
# seconds of execution on your machine.
total = 0
for i in range(30_000_000):
    total += i
total
```

<p>
  <button id="btn-terminate-python" class="webgeods-run-btn" style="background:#f85149;">■ Terminate Python (Runtime.terminatePython())</button>
</p>

<script>
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => {

  const counterEl = document.getElementById("heartbeat-counter");
  let ticks = 0;

  setInterval(() => {
    ticks += 1;
    counterEl.textContent = String(ticks);
  }, 300);

  document.getElementById("btn-terminate-python").onclick = () => {
    window.WebGeoDS.Runtime.terminatePython();
  };

});
</script>

## 13. R — separate stdout vs stderr, automatic `skipValueIfPrinted`

Verify two fixes together: `WebGeoDS.R.run()` now returns `stdout` and `stderr` as two separate arrays instead of a single stdout that merged them (`message()`/`warning()` end up on stderr in R, not stdout); and this cell **does not pass `{ skipValueIfPrinted: true }`** to `output.result()` — it must still work, because for a `language: "r"` cell it's now the automatic default (see `result()` in `code-cell.js`). No difference here compared to a hand-written cell: the filter still generates `output.result(await window.WebGeoDS.R.run(code, {}))`, without `skipValueIfPrinted`.

```{.webgeods-r #cell-r-stderr}
cat("Line on stdout via cat()\n")
message("Line on stderr via message()")
"final value"
```

## 14. R — explicit stop (`terminateR()`, not an in-place interrupt)

Verify the stop mechanism described in `runtime.js`: with the channel forced to `PostMessage`, there is no true mid-execution interrupt of an R computation via Atomics/SharedArrayBuffer; the only way to stop an in-progress R computation is to close and recreate the worker, exactly as `terminatePython()` already does for Python (with SharedArrayBuffer a real interrupt would in theory be possible, but that's not what we offer here, nor what this cell tests). Below is a dedicated "Terminate R" button, on the same pattern as §12's Python test (unlike that test, though, there's no need for a heartbeat counter here: webR already always runs in its own worker regardless of the channel, so the UI stays responsive even without this fix — what we're verifying here is only that the termination is clean).

```{.webgeods-r #cell-r-heavy}
# Heavy loop, deliberately slow: if it finishes before you manage to
# press "Terminate R" below, or takes more than a few seconds,
# adjust the number for your machine — R's interpreted loops
# are slow in a highly hardware-dependent way.
total <- 0
for (i in 1:20000000) {
  total <- total + i
}
total
```

<p>
  <button id="btn-terminate-r" class="webgeods-run-btn" style="background:#f85149;">■ Terminate R (Runtime.terminateR())</button>
</p>

<script>
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => {

  document.getElementById("btn-terminate-r").onclick = () => {
    window.WebGeoDS.Runtime.terminateR();
  };

});
</script>

## 15. OJS reactivity on cells generated by the Lua filter (`getCellValue`)

The cells generated by `webgeods-cells.lua` (all the ones on this page except §1, §9-§11) are pure `<div>` + `<script>` boilerplate — not reactive `{ojs}` blocks. They still become reactive toward downstream OJS cells **without touching the filter**: `WebGeoDSCodeCell.run()` unconditionally sets `this.element.value = result` and dispatches a real `"input"` event on its own container element after every Run (`code-cell.js`) — for **any** cell, hand-built or filter-generated, because it lives inside `run()`, not at construction time. `WebGeoDS.getCellValue(id, Generators)` — a plain function in `code-cell.js`, not a Quarto syntax shortcut — encapsulates the bridge to that event in a single hand-written line in the `.qmd`, one call per cell.

::: {.callout-important}
**Complete history (August 26, 2026) — three rounds of testing, and one consolidation.**

**First round** — dotless syntax (`{webgeods-py}`, like `{r}`/`{python}`/`{ojs}`): the cells appeared as literal text. Confirmed cause: Quarto recognizes `{r}`/`{python}`/`{ojs}` without a dot because they are registered execution engines (Jupyter/knitr), a different mechanism from the one Pandoc uses to assign classes to a fenced code block for a user Lua filter — that requires the dot (`.webgeods-py`). Fix applied, permanent.

**Second round** — with the correct syntax, an earlier version of the filter generated a reactive `{ojs}` block via `Generators.observe()` instead of today's boilerplate. The class was recognized and the filter really did generate that block — visible in the OJS source shown in the rendered page — but Quarto didn't execute it: it appeared as literal text, and downstream cells failed with `OJS Runtime Error ... is not defined`. Conclusion: an `{ojs}` block synthesized by a Lua filter never enters Quarto's OJS reactive graph, regardless of filter ordering — OJS extraction doesn't seem to operate on the post-filter AST. **The filter has not attempted OJS reactivity since**: it only generates `<div>` + `<script>`.

**Why `getCellValue()` uses `Generators.observe()` and not `viewof`/`Generators.input`:** an earlier version of this page (§10, removed on August 26, 2026 when this section was consolidated) hand-built a cell *inside* an `{ojs}` block with `viewof pyReattivo = { const cell = new WebGeoDS.CodeCell(...); await cell.ready(); return cell.element; }`, to test Observable's `viewof`/`Generators.input` convention. Real test (August 26, 2026): the downstream status element wasn't created at all until Run was pressed at least once — not a timing/scroll/focus issue, but the fact that `Generators.input` (used implicitly by `viewof`) only calls `change(value)` synchronously if `value !== undefined`, and for a hand-built `cell.element` that value is `undefined` until a real `"input"` event arrives. `Generators.observe()` doesn't have this problem: by calling `change(undefined)` explicitly as a first synchronous step, it immediately forces a downstream evaluation — that's why `getCellValue()` uses it.

**Third round — reactivity via `WebGeoDS.getCellValue()` (confirmed working):** the two `{ojs}` cells below the filter's cells read `run()`'s `"input"` event and feed `#lua-py-status`/`#lua-r-status`. If these two boxes appear right away when the page loads showing "no execution yet" and update on every Run, reactivity works for filter-generated cells too — without the filter itself ever needing to generate OJS.
:::

```{.webgeods-python #lua-py}
6 * 7
```

```{.webgeods-r #lua-r}
6 * 7
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
lua_py = WebGeoDS.getCellValue("lua-py", Generators)
```

```{ojs}

{
  const el = document.createElement("div");
  el.id = "lua-py-status";
  el.innerHTML = lua_py === undefined
    ? "<strong>Latest reactive value from the Python cell generated by the Lua filter (§15):</strong> <em>no execution yet — press ▶ Run above</em>"
    : `<strong>Latest reactive value from the Python cell generated by the Lua filter (§15):</strong> ${lua_py}`;
  return el;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
lua_r = WebGeoDS.getCellValue("lua-r", Generators)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const el = document.createElement("div");
  el.id = "lua-r-status";
  el.innerHTML = lua_r === undefined
    ? "<strong>Latest reactive value from the R cell generated by the Lua filter (§15):</strong> <em>no execution yet — press ▶ Run above</em>"
    : `<strong>Latest reactive value from the R cell generated by the Lua filter (§15):</strong> ${lua_r}`;

}
```

## 16. Python/R value conversion → JS (`getCellValue`)

Systematic check of how values returned by `{.webgeods-python}`/`{.webgeods-r}` cells reach OJS through `WebGeoDS.getCellValue()`. Each case is a triplet: a cell generated by the Lua filter (§15), an `{ojs}` cell that bridges via `getCellValue`, and a display-only `{ojs}` cell that uses the `describeValue()` helper defined below — it shows `typeof`, `Array.isArray`, and a JSON preview of the received value.

::: {.callout-note}
**Methodology and what to expect.** The Python cases (int/float/str/bool/list/dict) rely on Pyodide's implicit conversion plus `toTransferable()` in `runtime.js`, already read in the source this session — their outcome is "expected" and this section's job is to **confirm it** against a real browser. The `None` case is the trickiest: since `None → undefined`, the status box can't distinguish "the cell returned `None`" from "the cell has never been run" — both show `typeof === "undefined"`. This isn't a bug in this page, it's a direct consequence of the implementation choice; if the two cases ever need to be distinguished, an explicit sentinel value would have to be introduced (e.g. a cell that returns a `"__none__"` string instead of `None`), not resolved here.

The R cases (num/str/bool/vec/list/data.frame/NULL/sf) use `rObjectToNativeJs()` in `r.js`, which unlike the Python path **has no try/catch fallback** on the main conversion — if `.toJs()` throws an exception for a type it doesn't handle, the whole cell errors out instead of degrading to a string. Until August 25, 2026, `rObjectToNativeJs()` only unwrapped a simple single-element vector and returned `NULL`/`list()`/`data.frame()`/`sf` as webR's raw, intact `.toJs()` structure — a real test (August 26, 2026) confirmed that raw form exactly as described above, and in the process discovered it was silently discarding `names`: a `list(name = "Rome", population = 2873000)` became an anonymous array of `{type,names,values}` descriptors, with no way on the JS side to know which element was "name" and which was "population" without re-reading the internal structure.

**Improved on August 26, 2026, in direct response to this problem** (`rObjectToNativeJs()`/`convertRawRValue()` in `r.js`, rewritten): `NULL` now becomes a real JS `null` (no longer `{"type":"null"}`); `list()` and named vectors recompose `names`/`values` into a flat JS object — `list(name = "Rome", population = 2873000)` becomes `{name: "Rome", population: 2873000}`, directly readable. A `data.frame` follows the same logic (internally it's a `list` of columns in R) and becomes a **columnar** object with readable keys — `data.frame(name = c("Rome","Milan"), population = c(...))` becomes `{name: ["Rome","Milan"], population: [...]}` — not an array of per-row records: distinguishing a `data.frame` from an ordinary `list` would require reading the R attributes (`class`/`row.names`), which the webR dump used here doesn't carry. `sf` inherits the same improvement for ordinary columns (`name` → `"Rome"` instead of the raw descriptor), but the geometry column remains an array of raw coordinates with no geometry type or CRS — this limitation can't be solved on the JS side, because that information never crosses the conversion at all: see `conv-r-sf-geojson` below for the recommended pattern when clean GeoJSON is needed (explicit conversion on the R side, before the value leaves the cell).

**Verification status of this rewrite — confirmed on August 26, 2026 against a real Quarto render** (51/51 checks, including `conv-r-sf-geojson`): the logic had only been validated offline (`scratch/verify-r-convert.mjs`, against the exact JSON shapes confirmed in the previous test round), then a real run verified all four cases (`conv-r-null` → `null`, `conv-r-list`/`conv-r-df` → objects with the original keys, `conv-r-sf` → readable ordinary columns) exactly as predicted by the rewrite.

`conv-r-sf` declares its own `#| package: sf` **(fixed on August 26, 2026, after the first round of testing against a real Quarto render)**: the first version of this cell instead relied on §6 having already loaded `sf` elsewhere on the same page (the `WebGeoDS.Runtime` singleton persists installed packages across cells) — sound reasoning in isolation, but broken in practice by §14, which sits *between* §6 and this section in page order and calls `terminateR()`: the R worker gets closed and recreated from scratch, losing `sf` along with the rest of the R state. A real test did in fact show this cell failing with `there is no package called 'sf'` even after running §6 — not a bug in the filter or the singleton, but because neither one guarantees persistence *across* an explicit runtime termination. Declaring the package on the cell itself makes it self-sufficient regardless of the execution order of the other sections.

`conv-py-numpy` declares `#| package: numpy` **(fixed on August 26, 2026, after the first round of testing against a real Quarto render)**: the first version of this cell didn't declare it at all, relying on the claim — read in a JSDoc comment in `python.js`, never verified against a real browser until now — that `pyodide.runPythonAsync()` loads known packages referenced by an `import` in the code on its own. A real test instead showed `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'numpy'`: that behavior didn't occur (at least in this environment/version of Pyodide), so the claim was wrong or incomplete — the comment in `python.js` was corrected accordingly. Declaring the package explicitly with `#| package: numpy` is now the only verified way to make it work from a filter cell.

`conv-py-pandas`/`conv-py-geopandas` (added August 26, 2026): an initial real test confirmed that both degrade to a string (`typeof === "string"`, pandas' textual `repr()`) because neither `pandas.DataFrame` nor `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` is a native container (dict/list/set) or buffer-protocol like an ndarray, so `.toJs()` in `toTransferable()` (runtime.js) threw and it fell back to `String(value)` — for `geopandas` this meant geometry as literal text (`"POINT (...)"`) instead of coordinates.

**Improved on August 26, 2026, the same day, at the author's explicit request** ("can these types be improved to make them actually usable?" — it was no longer enough to confirm/document the degradation, it had to be fixed): `toTransferable()` in `runtime.js` now recognizes these two types *before* the generic fallback, by duck-typing on Python attributes (no `import pandas`/`import geopandas` on the worker side, so no new dependency). `pandas.DataFrame` (recognized by `.to_dict` + `.columns`, so as not to mistakenly catch a `Series`) is converted with `value.to_dict("records")` — an array of row objects, the most natural tabular shape on the JS side, instead of the textual repr(). `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` (recognized by `.crs` + `.to_json`) uses `value.to_json()` — which geopandas overrides to produce real GeoJSON — and `JSON.parse()`s the result: the geometry column therefore arrives as structured numeric coordinates inside a real `Feature`/`FeatureCollection` object, no longer text.

**CRS: same problem found on the R side, fixed here too (August 26, 2026).** The author empirically verified that `geojsonsf::sf_geojson()` (the R equivalent used in `conv-r-sf-geojson` below) doesn't reproject to WGS84 on its own — it writes the coordinates in the source CRS as-is. `GeoDataFrame.to_json()` has the same behavior (not documented here before this fix, by analogy with what was verified on the R side): without intervention, a `GeoDataFrame` in a CRS other than WGS84 would produce a syntactically valid GeoJSON with wrong coordinates. The difference from the R case is that here the conversion is **automatic** — it fires for any cell that returns a `GeoDataFrame`, without the author writing special code to trigger it — so the risk was more insidious (a GeoJSON that looks correct but is silently wrong, not an explicit step the author chooses and can control). Fix applied in `tryGeoDataFrameToGeoJson()`: if `.crs` is not `None`, we attempt `value.to_crs("EPSG:4326")` before `to_json()` (a harmless roundtrip if the CRS is already WGS84); if the reprojection fails (e.g. a CRS not recognized by pyproj) we fall back to the original value instead of failing the whole cell. Verified offline with a mock that the branch really reprojects before serializing, not the original object (`scratch/verify-py-transferable.mjs`, "non-WGS84 CRS" case).

**Verification status — confirmed on August 26, 2026 against a real Quarto render**: both `pandas.DataFrame` (via `to_dict("records")`) and `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` (via `to_crs("EPSG:4326")` + `to_json()`) behaved exactly as expected — an array of records for the former, a `FeatureCollection` with real numeric coordinates for the latter, both packages available in the tested environment. An honest caveat about the reprojection branch: the demo cell's `GeoDataFrame` object is already created in `EPSG:4326`, so this test confirms that `value.to_crs("EPSG:4326")` is called successfully (no exception, the value keeps flowing correctly through to the result) but not that a reprojection from a *different* CRS produces numerically correct coordinates — that specific case (verified only offline with a mock, `scratch/verify-py-transferable.mjs`) remains to be tried with a source object in a non-WGS84 CRS.

**Split display vs. saved value (added August 26, 2026, same day):** after seeing the converted output in `conv-py-pandas`/`conv-py-geopandas` for the first time in a real render, the author asked whether the cell could show the familiar native pandas table instead, while still converting the value used downstream. `runtime.js` now captures Python's own `str()` text (`captureDisplayText()`) on the *original* `DataFrame`/`GeoDataFrame` — the same aligned-column table a real Python REPL prints — separately from and before `toTransferable()` runs; `code-cell.js` shows that text in the cell's own output box when present. The value returned to `onRun`/OJS (`convPyPandas`/`convPyGeopandas` below, and everything downstream in this section) is untouched: still the converted array of records / `FeatureCollection`, exactly as described above. Only these two types are affected — every other cell on this page keeps showing its converted value exactly as before. Verified offline with mocks (`scratch/verify-py-transferable.mjs`, cases 5-8): the captured text and the converted value are independent when computed from the same mock object, and non-DataFrame/GeoDataFrame values never trigger `captureDisplayText()`. Not verified against a real Quarto render yet — the mock's `.toString()` return value is illustrative, not copied from real pandas/geopandas output, so the exact formatting (column alignment, index numbers) should be confirmed live.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
function describeValue(label, value, id) {
  const container = document.createElement("div");
  // The id is optional (default undefined = no id) but it's what lets
  // the Playwright smoke test (smoke-test.mjs) read each case's
  // result without doing textual parsing of the page.
  if (id) {
    container.id = id;
  }
  container.style.marginBottom = "0.6em";
  const type = value === null ? "null" : typeof value;
  const isArray = Array.isArray(value);
  let preview;
  try {
    preview = JSON.stringify(value);
    if (preview === undefined) {
      preview = String(value);
    }
  } catch (e) {
    preview = String(value);
  }
  if (preview && preview.length > 500) {
    preview = preview.slice(0, 500) + "… (truncated)";
  }
  container.innerHTML = `<strong>${label}:</strong> typeof=<code>${type}</code>, Array.isArray=<code>${isArray}</code><br><code>${preview}</code>`;
  return container;
}
```

`conv-r-sf-geojson` shows the recommended pattern when clean GeoJSON is needed from an `sf` cell (not solvable by the generic conversion above — see callout): the cell converts explicitly in R, before returning the value, instead of relying on `getCellValue()` to do it. **Updated on August 26, 2026, at the author's direct request**, replacing the first version (a hand-written `sprintf`, working only for single `POINT`s) with `geojsonsf::sf_geojson()` — a real function from the [geojsonsf](https://cran.r-project.org/package=geojsonsf) package, which correctly handles any geometry type (not just `POINT`) without needing to hand-branch on the type.

An important detail, verified by the author by running `sf_geojson()` directly in an `{r}` chunk (outside this system, in a normal R environment): the function **does not reproject** the `sf` object — it writes the coordinates as-is in the object's CRS, without converting them to WGS84. GeoJSON (RFC 7946), however, requires coordinates in WGS84 (EPSG:4326): if the source object is in a different CRS (e.g. a UTM projection or a national system), the resulting GeoJSON would have wrong coordinates — syntactically valid but geographically incorrect, with points ending up in the wrong place on a MapLibre map. The cell below therefore applies `sf::st_transform(x, 4326)` explicitly **before** `sf_geojson()`, unconditionally — a harmless no-op if the object is already in EPSG:4326 (as in the example here, where it wouldn't have changed anything), but necessary to make the pattern correct regardless of the starting CRS.

`geojsonsf` is a real, widely used CRAN package, but **its availability as a webR/WebAssembly binary is not verified in this sandbox** (the same limitation already hit for pandas/geopandas — no network access to `repo.r-wasm.org` from here): if the package weren't available in a given webR environment, the cell would fail to load — the smoke test treats this case as a valid observation, not an error (see `observePackageAvailability()` in `smoke-test.mjs`).

```{.webgeods-r #conv-r-sf-geojson}
#| package: sf, geojsonsf
pt <- sf::st_as_sf(data.frame(name = "Rome", lon = 12.4964, lat = 41.9028), coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
pt_wgs84 <- sf::st_transform(pt, 4326)
unname(geojsonsf::sf_geojson(pt_wgs84))
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
convRSfGeojsonText = WebGeoDS.getCellValue("conv-r-sf-geojson", Generators)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// The R cell returns ready-made GeoJSON text (a string) — the
// parsing happens here on the OJS side, not in the R cell, to keep
// "generate valid GeoJSON" (the R cell's responsibility) separate
// from "parse it as an object" (the consumer's responsibility).
// Before the first Run convRSfGeojsonText is undefined: the guard
// below stops JSON.parse from throwing in that case, showing the
// raw value instead of an error.
convRSfGeojson = {
  if (typeof convRSfGeojsonText !== "string") {
    return convRSfGeojsonText;
  }
  try {
    return JSON.parse(convRSfGeojsonText);
  } catch (e) {
    return convRSfGeojsonText;
  }
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
describeValue("R — sf explicitly converted to GeoJSON via geojsonsf, with an explicit st_transform(4326) before the conversion — see callout above", convRSfGeojson, "conv-r-sf-geojson-desc")
```

## Manual verification checklist

- **Runtime (§1):** initial state `idle`/`idle`; clicking "Load Python"/"Load R" moves the state to `loading` then `ready`; "Terminate" brings it back to `idle`; the panel updates on its own (`statuschange` event), no need to reload the page. "Load R" explicitly forces the `PostMessage` channel (see `_loadR()` in `runtime.js`) instead of leaving auto-detection to webR — identical behavior across every hosting platform, since Teachable would pick PostMessage anyway for lack of custom headers. A real test initially showed §5/§6/§13 losing multi-line output with this forcing active, but the real cause wasn't the channel: `shelter.captureR()` defaults to `withAutoprint: false` (verified against the webR v0.6.0 source), which suppresses any auto-printed value on any channel. Fix in r.js (`{ withAutoprint: true }`); the channel forcing was reapplied.
- **Python basics (§2):** `stdout` shows the `print()` line, then `Output: 42`.
- **Python + package (§3):** both `print()` lines appear in the correct order; `Output: ...` must show the array `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` in JSON format — not `{}` (a regression not to reintroduce: a Pyodide `PyProxy`, e.g. a NumPy ndarray, must be converted with `.toJs()` before `JSON.stringify`). `#| package: numpy` must not show up in the editor as that line (the filter strips it) and must not cause abnormal loading delays.
- **Python error (§4):** the output moves to `error` state (red) with the Python exception message.
- **R basics (§5):** `cat()` appears in stdout, followed by the auto-print of `1:5`; no extra `Output:` line — and note that this cell no longer passes `{ skipValueIfPrinted: true }` to `output.result()`: it's automatic for `language: "r"` cells.
- **R + sf (§6):** **only** the `sf` table printed by R appears — no duplicate JSON block below (a regression not to reintroduce). `#| package: sf` must install the package even if this is the first R cell run on the page (must not depend on any other cell).
- **R invisible (§7):** no auto-print in stdout, but `Output: 42` appears.
- **R error (§8):** `error` state with the message passed to `stop()`.
- **Manual CellOutput (§9):** the two "waiting" messages replace each other; the success message stays visible along with the green node added via `append()`.
- **Basic map (§10):** three visible layers (orange points, blue line, semi-transparent light-blue polygon); "Add Turin" makes a fourth point appear and the view refits; "Remove link" makes the line disappear; "Narrow/widen + resize()" visibly changes the map's width and shows a green log below the buttons, "✓ resize() executed without errors..." (red if it throws an exception); "Test error" shows an alert with an error message, not an unhandled exception in the console.
- **Custom map style (§11):** the second map uses a light style (Alidade Smooth) instead of the default dark background, confirming that the `style` option is respected.
- **Python in a Web Worker (§12):** press Run on the heavy cell and watch the counter — it must keep rising for the whole duration of the execution, with no stutters or freezes (otherwise Pyodide has gone back to running on the main thread). Halfway through, press "■ Terminate Python": the cell's output must move to an error state (not stay stuck on "Running...") and the Run button must become clickable again. After termination, verify that re-running any Python cell (e.g. §2) still works — it must recreate a new worker transparently.
- **R — stdout vs stderr (§13):** `message()` appears in a separate "⚠ stderr:" block, distinct from the `cat()` line and the auto-print of the final value (both of which remain in stdout); no extra `Output:` line, even though this cell doesn't declare `skipValueIfPrinted` — confirming that the automatic default for R works without needing the explicit flag. This cell also served as an unintentional regression test for the real August 25, 2026 bug (`withAutoprint: false` by default in `shelter.captureR()`, see §1): before the fix in r.js, only the `cat()` line survived in `capture.output`, and `message()` and the auto-print disappeared entirely — if they go missing again, it's the same symptom, and it's worth checking the `withAutoprint` option in r.js first, not the channel.
- **R — explicit stop (§14):** press Run on the heavy cell, then halfway through press "■ Terminate R": the output must move to an error state (not stay stuck on "Running...") and the Run button must become clickable again — the same guarantee already verified for Python in §12. No true in-place interrupt, since the channel is forced to PostMessage (see §1); after termination, verify that re-running any R cell (e.g. §5) still works — it must recreate a new worker transparently.
- **Reactivity on Lua filter cells (§15):** `#lua-py-status`/`#lua-r-status` must be visible **right away when the page loads**, before pressing Run, showing "no execution yet" — this is the direct verification that `Generators.observe()` propagates an initial value immediately, unlike `viewof`/`Generators.input` (history in the section's callout). After Run on each cell (`#lua-py`, `#lua-r`), the corresponding box must update to `42`.
- **Python/R → JS conversion (§16):** every cell is self-sufficient (`conv-r-sf` declares `#| package: sf`, `conv-r-sf-geojson` declares `#| package: sf, geojsonsf` — they no longer depend on §6, see the callout at the top of §16 for why this was fixed), so the cells can be run in any order, even after §14.
